title: ReLoop-UME: Recurrent Depth with Learnable Retrieval Registers for Universal Multimodal Embedding
summary: Universal multimodal embedding (UME) maps heterogeneous multimodal inputs into a shared embedding space. Existing UME models either form embeddings through single forward encoding or add computation through explicit rationale tokens and latent autoregressive states. Although token expansion can improve complex matching, serial generation increases retrieval latency and makes the final embedding depend on generated intermediate states. This raises a different question: can useful computation be expanded along model depth while keeping the token workspace fixed? We analyze positive-negative similarity separation at every layer of independently trained UME models and observe a shared progression: early layers contextualize multimodal inputs, a contiguous middle-to-late stage forms retrieval-discriminative features, and the final layers map them into the embedding space. Based on this finding, we propose ReLoop-UME, which executes the early layers once, recurrently reuses a parameter-shared retrieval-forming block, and applies the final mapping layers after the last loop. Learnable Retrieval Registers provide persistent retrieval-specific states that accumulate and exchange evidence across loops, with the final register serving as the embedding readout. On MMEB-V2 and MRMR, ReLoop-UME consistently improves retrieval across different backbones while running 44.9x faster than UME-R1 and 1.5x faster than PLUME.

AI.tldr: ReLoop-UME expands computation for universal multimodal embedding along model depth via recurrent reuse of a parameter-shared retrieval-forming block, rather than serial token expansion, achieving faster and better retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing UME models either use single forward encoding (limited computation for complex matching) or token expansion with serial generation (slow retrieval and embeddings depend on generated intermediate states). The paper asks whether useful computation can be expanded along model depth while keeping the token workspace fixed.
AI.method: Analyze layer-wise positive-negative similarity separation in trained UME models, finding three stages: early contextualization, middle-to-late retrieval-discriminative feature formation, and final embedding mapping. Based on this, ReLoop-UME executes early layers once, recurrently reuses a parameter-shared retrieval-forming block, and applies final mapping layers after the last loop. Learnable Retrieval Registers provide persistent retrieval-specific states that accumulate and exchange evidence across loops, with the final register serving as embedding readout.
AI.result: On MMEB-V2 and MRMR benchmarks, ReLoop-UME consistently improves retrieval across different backbones while running 44.9x faster than UME-R1 and 1.5x faster than PLUME.
AI.conclusion: Expanding computation along depth via recurrent parameter-shared blocks offers a faster and effective alternative to serial token expansion for multimodal embedding retrieval.

title: SCMA: Structure-Conditioned and Metal-Aware Flow Matching for CT Metal Artifact Reduction
summary: In X-ray CT, metallic objects cause beam hardening, photon starvation, and scattering, leading to projection inconsistency, streaks, dark bands, and structural distortions that compromise clinical diagnosis and quantitative analysis. Existing metal artifact reduction (MAR) methods remain limited: optimization-based methods may leave residual artifacts or blur structures, regression networks may generalize poorly across scenarios, and generative models without sample-specific structural guidance and physical constraints may produce anatomically inconsistent structures. Flow Matching learns a continuous-time velocity field that deterministically transports a source distribution to a target distribution, providing a flexible MAR prior. However, standard unconditional Flow Matching does not exploit sample-specific structure, spatially nonuniform metal-induced degradation, or measured projections. To address these limitations, we propose SCMA, a structure-conditioned and metal-aware Flow Matching framework. First, a linear-interpolation-corrected image is fed into the velocity network with the intermediate state as a sample-specific structural condition, guiding inference toward artifact-free CT images while preserving anatomy. Second, time-varying spatial weights from the metal mask and its distance transform are incorporated into the Flow Matching loss to emphasize severe degradation within and around metal regions. Finally, conditional Flow Matching updates alternate with projection-consistency correction during inference, allowing reliable measurements outside metal traces to constrain predictions. Experiments on simulated and real CT data demonstrate that SCMA more effectively suppresses metal artifacts, preserves local anatomical structures, and reduces hallucination-like structures inconsistent with projection measurements than representative MAR methods.

AI.tldr: SCMA is a structure-conditioned and metal-aware Flow Matching framework for metal artifact reduction (MAR) in X-ray CT, combining sample-specific structural conditioning, time-varying spatial weighting from metal masks, and alternating projection-consistency correction during inference to suppress artifacts while preserving anatomy.
AI.motivation: Existing MAR methods (optimization-based, regression networks, generative models) have limitations: residual artifacts, poor generalization, and anatomically inconsistent structures. Standard Flow Matching provides a flexible prior but fails to exploit sample-specific structure, spatially nonuniform degradation, or measured projections.
AI.method: Three key components: (1) a linear-interpolation-corrected image is fed into the velocity network with the intermediate state as a sample-specific structural condition; (2) time-varying spatial weights derived from the metal mask and its distance transform are incorporated into the Flow Matching loss to emphasize severe degradation near metals; (3) conditional Flow Matching updates alternate with projection-consistency correction during inference.
AI.result: Experiments on simulated and real CT data show SCMA suppresses metal artifacts more effectively, preserves local anatomical structures better, and reduces hallucination-like structures inconsistent with projection measurements compared to representative MAR methods.
AI.conclusion: SCMA demonstrates that integrating sample-specific structural guidance, metal-aware weighting, and projection consistency into Flow Matching yields superior metal artifact reduction while preserving anatomical fidelity.

title: WaiT for the Signal: Simple Frequency-Aware Flow-Matching
summary: As image generation models scale to ever higher resolutions, global coherence, local detail, and texture fidelity become critical axes for generation quality. However, standard flow matching treats all spatial frequencies uniformly, ignoring the natural frequency hierarchy where high-frequency bands become indistinguishable from pure noise far earlier than coarse structures. We introduce WaiT, a Wavelet-aware image Transformer that decomposes generation into coarse and fine bands via lossless wavelets. True to its name, the high-frequency bands wait for the signal: staying pure noise until coarse structure has emerged, then joining the flow for joint refinement. Since standard FID discards fine-grained detail through aggressive downsampling, we introduce a more stringent three-axis evaluation protocol to assess quality at native resolution. On ImageNet 512x512, WaiT achieves a pixel-space FID of 1.43 and is Pareto-optimal across all three axes, reducing sampling compute by up to 50%. With our largest 2B model, we set a new state-of-the-art FID of 1.3 for pixel-space models on ImageNet 512 resolution. Our formulation outperforms even the strongest latent-space models on texture fidelity, and scales seamlessly to high-resolution OpenImages and to video generation, achieving a state-of-the-art FVD of 0.84 on Kinetics-600 with no algorithmic modifications.

AI.tldr: WaiT is a Wavelet-aware image Transformer that decomposes generation into coarse and fine bands via lossless wavelets, where high-frequency bands remain pure noise until coarse structure emerges. It achieves state-of-the-art FID of 1.3 at 512x512 on ImageNet with 50% less sampling compute, and scales to video generation with FVD 0.84 on Kinetics-600.
AI.motivation: Standard flow matching treats all spatial frequencies uniformly, ignoring the natural frequency hierarchy where high-frequency bands become indistinguishable from pure noise far earlier than coarse structures. This leads to inefficiencies and suboptimal generation quality at high resolutions.
AI.method: WaiT decomposes image generation into coarse and fine bands using lossless wavelets. High-frequency bands "wait" as pure noise until coarse structure has emerged, then join the flow for joint refinement. A new three-axis evaluation protocol is introduced to assess quality at native resolution since standard FID discards fine-grained detail through aggressive downsampling.
AI.result: On ImageNet 512x512, WaiT achieves pixel-space FID of 1.43 and is Pareto-optimal across all three evaluation axes, reducing sampling compute by up to 50%. The largest 2B model sets a new SOTA FID of 1.3 for pixel-space models on ImageNet 512. It outperforms even the strongest latent-space models on texture fidelity and achieves SOTA FVD of 0.84 on Kinetics-600 for video generation.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the frequency hierarchy in generation through wavelets yields significant improvements in quality, efficiency, and scalability—surpassing pixel-space and even latent-space models—and extends seamlessly to video generation without algorithmic changes.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Deepfake Detection via Multi-View Structural Learning
summary: Security-critical biometric and forensic applications require accurate predictions and reliable confidence estimates, particularly under distribution shift. This challenge is especially acute for deepfake detection, where foundation-model-based detectors often exhibit overconfident predictions on out-of-distribution manipulations, which limits their suitability for operational deployment. We propose an uncertainty-aware deepfake detection framework that identifies manipulations through inconsistencies across complementary evidence sources. The framework integrates three streams: a visual stream based on an adapted CLIP encoder, a semantic stream that models consistency among facial attributes through differentiable constraints, and a structural stream that captures class-dependent dependency patterns between semantic and forensic features. To effectively combine these signals, we introduce Inter-Branch Disagreement Calibration (IBDC), a disagreement-aware uncertainty modeling mechanism that links predictive uncertainty to conflicts among evidence streams. Extensive cross-dataset experiments using FaceForensics++ as the training source demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art generalization across multiple out-of-distribution benchmarks while consistently improving calibration and selective prediction performance. These results show that combining complementary evidence with disagreement-aware uncertainty provides a robust foundation for trustworthy and well-calibrated deepfake detection under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an uncertainty-aware deepfake detection framework that integrates three complementary evidence streams (visual CLIP-based, semantic facial-attribute consistency, and structural dependency patterns) with an Inter-Branch Disagreement Calibration (IBDC) mechanism to link predictive uncertainty to conflicts among evidence streams, achieving state-of-the-art generalization, calibration, and selective prediction under distribution shift.
AI.motivation: Deepfake detectors, particularly foundation-model-based ones, suffer from overconfident predictions on out-of-distribution manipulations, making them unreliable for security-critical operational deployment where accurate predictions and calibrated confidence estimates are essential.
AI.method: The framework integrates three evidence streams: (1) a visual stream using an adapted CLIP encoder, (2) a semantic stream modeling facial attribute consistency through differentiable constraints, and (3) a structural stream capturing class-dependent dependency patterns between semantic and forensic features. These are combined via Inter-Branch Disagreement Calibration (IBDC), a disagreement-aware uncertainty modeling mechanism that ties predictive uncertainty to conflicts among evidence streams.
AI.result: Cross-dataset experiments trained on FaceForensics++ show state-of-the-art generalization across multiple out-of-distribution benchmarks, with consistently improved calibration and selective prediction performance compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Combining complementary evidence with disagreement-aware uncertainty provides a robust foundation for trustworthy and well-calibrated deepfake detection under distribution shift, making the approach suitable for operational security-critical applications.

title: Do Medical Foundation Models Generalize on the African Brain?
comment: Submitted to the AFRICAI workshop (Held in conjunction with MICCAI 2026, Strasbourg, France)
summary: Medical foundation models (FMs) are increasingly used for brain MRI analysis. However, their evaluation remains dominated by high-resource datasets, leaving generalization to African cohorts underexplored. We assess whether FMs generalize equally to African and non-African brain MRI data across two tasks: dementia classification using a Nigerian dataset and brain tumor segmentation using BraTS-Africa. We evaluate two generalist FMs (BrainIAC, 3DINO) and two segmentation-specific FMs (MedSAM2, Medical-SAM2) against a from-scratch baseline. For classification, FMs provide limited gains (highest ROC-AUC of 0.86 with BrainIAC), whereas for segmentation they consistently improve performance, reaching up to 0.86 Dice with MedSAM2. Performance differences between African and non-African cohorts are inconsistent and appear more related to dataset size than data origin. These results suggest that FMs do not exhibit an inherent bias against African cohorts, and highlight the limited availability and diversity of African neuroimaging datasets as the main barrier to robust evaluation and deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether medical foundation models (FMs) generalize equally to African and non-African brain MRI data, testing two generalist FMs (BrainIAC, 3DINO) and two segmentation-specific FMs (MedSAM2, Medical-SAM2) on dementia classification (Nigerian dataset) and brain tumor segmentation (BraTS-Africa). FMs provide limited gains in classification (best ROC-AUC 0.86) but consistently improve segmentation (best Dice 0.86). Performance differences between African and non-African cohorts are inconsistent and more related to dataset size than data origin, suggesting FMs lack inherent bias against African cohorts. The main barrier is limited availability and diversity of African neuroimaging datasets.
AI.motivation: Medical foundation models for brain MRI are increasingly common, but their evaluation has been dominated by high-resource datasets, leaving questions about whether they generalize well to African cohorts largely unexplored. This is an important gap given potential deployment in diverse global populations.
AI.method: The authors evaluate four foundation models (two generalist: BrainIAC, 3DINO; two segmentation-specific: MedSAM2, Medical-SAM2) against a from-scratch baseline. They test these models on two tasks: (1) dementia classification using a Nigerian dataset and (2) brain tumor segmentation using BraTS-Africa, comparing performance across African and non-African cohorts.
AI.result: For classification, FMs provide limited gains with the highest ROC-AUC of 0.86 achieved by BrainIAC. For segmentation, FMs consistently improve performance, reaching up to 0.86 Dice with MedSAM2. Performance differences between African and non-African cohorts are inconsistent and appear more related to dataset size than data origin.
AI.conclusion: Foundation models do not exhibit an inherent bias against African cohorts. The primary barrier to robust evaluation and deployment is the limited availability and diversity of African neuroimaging datasets rather than model bias.

title: Can Synthetic Data Overcome the Generalization Limits of AI-Based Flower and Pod Detection Across Cowpea Breeding Genotypes and Environments?
summary: High-throughput phenotyping requires AI-enabled computer vision models that generalize across genotypes, locations, and growing seasons, yet such models often lose accuracy under new conditions. Annotating real imagery for every genotype-by-environment (G x E) combination a breeding program encounters is prohibitively expensive. We quantify how G x E shifts affect AI-based detection of cowpea flowers and pods across two California locations and two growing seasons. Flower detection mAP@50 fell from 76.3% to as low as 50.6% under unseen shifts, and pod detection was more sensitive. Feature-space and image-quality diagnostics confirmed these losses track measurable distributional shifts. Because closing this gap with real data alone is not practical, we test whether synthetic imagery, rendered from a procedural 3D cowpea model, can substitute for that annotation burden. Synthetic supervision alone improved over pretraining but remained limited by a domain gap driven by camera image formation, not scene content. A domain-gap-aware camera-realism augmentation strategy, optimized against measured real-image statistics via Wasserstein distance, narrowed this gap, and a linear HDR representation converted a smaller measured gap into a larger detection gain than an 8-bit representation. Optimized HDR synthetic data combined with as few as five real images matched or exceeded the real-data baseline for spatial generalization, and pod detection benefited most at the lowest shot counts, with more modest gains under temporal shift. These results show that synthetic data can overcome the generalization limits of AI-based flower and pod detection, but only when the domain gap is measured and optimized rather than assumed away.

AI.tldr: This paper quantifies how genotype-by-environment (G x E) shifts degrade AI-based cowpea flower and pod detection (mAP@50 dropping from 76.3% to 50.6%), and demonstrates that procedurally rendered synthetic imagery—combined with a domain-gap-aware camera-realism augmentation strategy optimized via Wasserstein distance and linear HDR representation—can match or exceed real-data baselines using as few as five real images.
AI.motivation: AI models for high-throughput plant phenotyping often fail to generalize across genotypes, locations, and growing seasons. Annotating real imagery for every G x E combination is prohibitively expensive, so there is a practical need to quantify these distributional shifts and find alternative data sources (i.e., synthetic imagery) to close the generalization gap.
AI.method: The authors quantify G x E shifts on cowpea flower and pod detection across two California locations and two seasons. They use a procedural 3D cowpea model to render synthetic imagery for supervision, and apply a domain-gap-aware camera-realism augmentation strategy optimized against real-image statistics using Wasserstein distance. They also compare 8-bit versus linear HDR image representations and evaluate few-shot scenarios with as few as five real images combined with synthetic data.
AI.result: Synthetic supervision alone improved over pretraining but was limited by a domain gap driven by camera image formation. The optimized HDR synthetic data combined with five real images matched or exceeded the real-data baseline for spatial generalization; pod detection benefited most at low shot counts, while gains under temporal shift were more modest.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic data can overcome generalization limits of AI-based flower and pod detection, but only when the domain gap is explicitly measured and optimized (e.g., via Wasserstein-based augmentation and HDR representation) rather than assumed to be negligible.

title: FocusGS: Spatial Delta Layers for Local Repair and Deterministic Editing of Trained 3D Gaussian Assets
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Ancillary demonstration video included
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is evolving from one-time reconstruction into deliverable, inspectable, and maintainable visual assets. Existing workflows focus on global reconstruction, training-time density control, or open-ended generative editing, leaving trained assets without precise local maintenance. We propose FocusGS, which unifies local repair and deterministic editing as composite spatial deltas. Repair is the purely additive special case: its base-manipulation term is empty, and it adds only local Gaussian bases; deterministic editing uses erase-insert factorization (EIF) to combine old-carrier erasure with new-content insertion. FocusGS addresses spatial gradient starvation: local repair raises target-region PSNR by 7.91 dB over 93 evaluation views. Across all 83 deterministic editing trials, the target ROI improves, with a trial-averaged mean edited ROI PSNR of 21.97 dB and a mean gain of +11.05 dB; across five public editing cases, FocusGS-EIF reaches 33.17 dB Target-mask PSNR and 0.994 Target-delta Correlation, while both text-driven baselines fail to complete the prescribed updates. FocusGS provides a lightweight, verifiable 3DGS maintenance operator.

AI.tldr: FocusGS is a 3D Gaussian Splatting maintenance operator that unifies local repair and deterministic editing through composite spatial deltas, achieving significant improvements in target-region quality (7.91 dB for repair, +11.05 dB for editing) over existing global reconstruction and training-time density control approaches.
AI.motivation: 3DGS is evolving from one-time reconstruction into maintainable visual assets, but existing workflows lack precise local maintenance capabilities—they focus on global reconstruction, training-time density control, or open-ended generative editing, leaving trained assets without mechanisms for surgical local repair or deterministic editing.
AI.method: FocusGS unifies local repair and deterministic editing as composite spatial deltas. Repair is a purely additive special case with an empty base-manipulation term that only adds local Gaussian bases. Deterministic editing uses erase-insert factorization (EIF), which combines old-carrier erasure with new-content insertion. The method also addresses spatial gradient starvation that limits effective local updates.
AI.result: Local repair improves target-region PSNR by 7.91 dB over 93 evaluation views. Across 83 deterministic editing trials, the target ROI consistently improves with a trial-averaged mean edited ROI PSNR of 21.97 dB and mean gain of +11.05 dB. Across five public editing cases, FocusGS-EIF achieves 33.17 dB Target-mask PSNR and 0.994 Target-delta Correlation, while text-driven baselines fail to complete prescribed updates.
AI.conclusion: FocusGS provides a lightweight, verifiable 3DGS maintenance operator that enables precise local repair and deterministic editing, filling the gap between global reconstruction and generative editing workflows.

title: A Unified Benchmark of Deep Learning Models for Multi-task 3D Brain Tumor Segmentation from Magnetic Resonance Imaging
comment: 27 pages, 16 figures, 8 tables
summary: Automatic brain tumor segmentation from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has become a fundamental task in computer-assisted diagnosis, treatment planning, and disease monitoring. Although numerous deep learning architectures have recently been proposed, objective comparisons remain challenging because published studies often employ different datasets, preprocessing strategies, training protocols, and evaluation procedures. This work presents a unified experimental benchmark for comparing representative convolutional neural networks (CNNs), Transformer-based models, and recent State Space Model (SSM) architectures under homogeneous experimental conditions. Five state-of-the-art three-dimensional segmentation models, including 3D U-Net, SegResNet, Swin UNETR, SegMamba, and SegMambaV2, are evaluated on two brain tumor segmentation datasets representing distinct clinical scenarios: intracranial meningioma segmentation (BraTS 2023) and post-treatment glioma segmentation (BraTS 2024). All architectures are trained using identical preprocessing, data augmentation, optimization strategies, and evaluation protocols to ensure a fair comparison. Performance is assessed using segmentation accuracy metrics together with computational cost indicators, including inference time and the size of each model. The results provide practical insights into the trade-offs between segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency, highlighting the suitability of different architectural paradigms for challenging three-dimensional brain tumor segmentation tasks.

AI.tldr: A unified benchmark comparing five 3D brain tumor segmentation models (3D U-Net, SegResNet, Swin UNETR, SegMamba, SegMambaV2) across CNNs, Transformers, and SSM architectures under identical experimental conditions on two BraTS datasets (2023 meningioma, 2024 glioma).
AI.motivation: Objective comparisons of brain tumor segmentation deep learning models are difficult because published studies use inconsistent datasets, preprocessing, training protocols, and evaluation procedures, making it hard to determine which architectures truly perform best.
AI.method: Five representative 3D segmentation models spanning three architectural paradigms (CNNs: 3D U-Net, SegResNet; Transformers: Swin UNETR; SSM: SegMamba, SegMambaV2) are evaluated on two brain tumor datasets under homogeneous preprocessing, augmentation, optimization, and evaluation protocols. Performance is measured using segmentation accuracy metrics plus computational cost indicators (inference time, model size).
AI.result: The benchmark yields practical insights into accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across architectural paradigms, highlighting which model types are best suited for challenging 3D brain tumor segmentation tasks.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a fair, standardized experimental setup for comparing NN architectures in 3D brain tumor segmentation, offering guidance on balancing segmentation accuracy against computational efficiency for different clinical scenarios.

title: Physics-Aligned Self-Supervised Learning for Scientific Imaging
summary: Data augmentations define the invariances learned by self-supervised learning (SSL). Standard augmentation pipelines were designed for natural images, yet scientific imaging modalities are governed by physical measurement processes with distinct symmetry and acquisition constraints. Enforcing invariances that contradict these constraints can distort learned representations and limit downstream performance, but practitioners moving from machine learning into a new scientific modality currently have little guidance beyond transferring natural-image pipelines unexamined. We address this gap with a principled, reproducible procedure for augmentation design in scientific SSL: we formalise the physics-aligned augmentation set as a union of measurement-consistent symmetries and acquisition-driven perturbations, and we give a concrete, largely label-free workflow---enumerate candidates, label each by the measurement operator, validate with representation-geometry diagnostics, and confirm by single-factor ablation---for selecting them. We instantiate the procedure for real-space electron microscopy and reciprocal-space 4D-STEM diffraction, and evaluate it across five SSL paradigms (DINOv2, SimCLR, MAE, VICRegL, I-JEPA) on classification and crystal-orientation regression. Physics-aligned augmentations substantially improve downstream performance for objectives relying on cross-view consistency, reduce geodesic error and improve robustness under realistic acquisition variability (detector gain, resolution loss), and systematically reshape representation geometry. While our experiments use electron microscopy, the procedure is modality-agnostic and applies to other measurement-driven domains such as medical and remote-sensing imaging. These results position augmentation design as a primary, and controllable, source of inductive bias in scientific self-supervised learning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a principled, reproducible procedure for designing physics-aligned data augmentations in scientific self-supervised learning (SSL), formalized as a union of measurement-consistent symmetries and acquisition-driven perturbations. The workflow—enumerate candidates, label by measurement operator, validate with representation-geometry diagnostics, confirm by single-factor ablation—is instantiated for electron microscopy and 4D-STEM, and evaluated across five SSL paradigms, showing improved downstream performance, reduced geodesic error, and robustness under realistic acquisition variability.
AI.motivation: Standard augmentation pipelines designed for natural images do not transfer well to scientific imaging modalities governed by physical measurement processes, and practitioners lack guidance for designing augmentations that respect physical constraints. Misaligned invariances can distort learned representations and hurt downstream performance.
AI.method: The authors formalize the physics-aligned augmentation set as a union of measurement-consistent symmetries and acquisition-driven perturbations, and propose a largely label-free workflow: enumerate augmentation candidates, label each by the measurement operator, validate with representation-geometry diagnostics, and confirm by single-factor ablation. They instantiate this for real-space electron microscopy and reciprocal-space 4D-STEM, testing across DINOv2, SimCLR, MAE, VICRegL, and I-JEPA on classification and crystal-orientation regression.
AI.result: Physics-aligned augmentations substantially improve downstream performance for objectives relying on cross-view consistency, reduce geodesic error, improve robustness under realistic acquisition variability (detector gain, resolution loss), and systematically reshape representation geometry across five SSL paradigms.
AI.conclusion: Augmentation design should be treated as a primary, controllable source of inductive bias in scientific SSL. Though demonstrated on electron microscopy, the proposed procedure is modality-agnostic and applicable to other measurement-driven domains such as medical and remote-sensing imaging.

title: Group-wise Supervision with Focal-Dice Loss for Long-Tailed Indoor Semantic Occupancy Prediction
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures
summary: Recently, 3D semantic occupancy prediction has garnered increasing attention for understanding the indoor scene. However, unlike structured outdoor environments, indoor scenes feature a high diversity of object categories that exhibit a severe long-tailed distribution, which has become a core bottleneck limiting the performance of existing models. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel method, Group-UFD Occ, based on hierarchical semantic supervision and synergistic loss optimization. At the architectural level, we introduce a fine-grained semantic grouping strategy and design multi-scale, parallel ``main-expert'' prediction heads to guide the model in efficiently learning tail-class features through deep regularization. At the optimization level, we introduce the Unified Focal-Dice (UFD) loss. This synergistic loss function dynamically focuses on hard samples at the per-voxel level. Meanwhile, it simultaneously optimizes the geometric integrity of predicted objects from a region-based perspective. We conducted experiments on the large-scale EmbodiedScan dataset. The results demonstrate that our method yields a relative improvement of 11.38\% over the baseline, with substantial accuracy gains in several critical long-tailed categories.

AI.tldr: Group-UFD Occ is a novel 3D semantic occupancy prediction method for indoor scenes that addresses the long-tailed distribution problem through hierarchical semantic supervision and a synergistic Unified Focal-Dice (UFD) loss, achieving an 11.38% relative improvement over baseline on the EmbodiedScan dataset.
AI.motivation: Indoor scenes have high diversity of object categories with a severe long-tailed distribution, which is a core bottleneck limiting the performance of existing 3D semantic occupancy prediction models.
AI.method: Two main contributions: (1) At the architectural level, a fine-grained semantic grouping strategy with multi-scale parallel "main-expert" prediction heads to efficiently learn tail-class features through deep regularization. (2) At the optimization level, the Unified Focal-Dice (UFD) loss that dynamically focuses on hard samples at the per-voxel level while simultaneously optimizing geometric integrity of predicted objects from a region-based perspective.
AI.result: Experiments on the large-scale EmbodiedScan dataset show a relative improvement of 11.38% over the baseline, with substantial accuracy gains in several critical long-tailed categories.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Group-UFD Occ method effectively tackles the long-tailed distribution challenge in indoor 3D semantic occupancy prediction through combined architectural and optimization-level innovations.

title: DiffAttack: Evasion Attacks Against Face Recognition via Latent Diffusion Models
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Joint Conference on Biometrics (IJCB) 2026
summary: Facial biometric identification relies on the distinctiveness of user attributes within a high-dimensional embedding space. However, the decision boundaries of deep face recognition (FR) systems are often sufficiently narrow that they can be conflated, rendering the models vulnerable to adversarial attacks. In such scenarios, the FR system fails to distinguish between an authentic source and a meticulously crafted adversarial face. Existing adversarial methods targeting facial biometrics are limited in both performance and their ability to generate high-quality images that are imperceptible to humans. Moreover, these methods often fail when the source and target images belong to different demographic groups or genders. To address these limitations, we present a novel approach for adversarial face generation via latent-space optimization. We leverage latent diffusion models directly to guide generation toward target identity embeddings, as measured by a face recognition model. Our proposed \textbf{DiffAttack} framework has been evaluated on standard benchmarks, such as the FFHQ and CelebA-HQ datasets. DiffAttack significantly outperforms existing adversarial techniques, achieving a high average attack success rate of 84.86% across multiple face recognition models (e.g., FaceNet). Notably, DiffAttack demonstrates superior transferability, surpassing traditional noise-based methods by over 15.28% and semantic-based approaches by approximately 5.21% on benchmark datasets like FFHQ and CelebA-HQ.

AI.tldr: DiffAttack is a novel adversarial face generation framework that uses latent diffusion models and latent-space optimization to create high-quality, imperceptible adversarial faces targeting FR systems, achieving 84.86% average attack success rate and superior transferability across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Deep face recognition systems have narrow decision boundaries that are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, but existing adversarial methods for facial biometrics are limited in performance, image quality, and fail across demographic groups or genders.
AI.method: The proposed DiffAttack framework leverages latent diffusion models to guide adversarial face generation toward target identity embeddings via latent-space optimization, measured by a face recognition model.
AI.result: DiffAttack achieves 84.86% average attack success rate across multiple FR models, outperforming noise-based methods by over 15.28% and semantic-based approaches by ~5.21% on FFHQ and CelebA-HQ datasets.
AI.conclusion: Latent diffusion-based adversarial face generation significantly improves attack success rate, transferability, and image quality over existing methods, addressing limitations related to cross-demographic and cross-gender attacks.

title: Automated classification method of COVID-19 cases from chest CT volumes using 2D and 3D hybrid CNN for anisotropic volumes
comment: Oral Presentation in SPIE Medical Imaging 2022
summary: This paper proposes an automated classification method of chest CT volumes based on likelihood of COVID-19 cases. Novel coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) spreads over the world, causing a large number of infected patients and deaths. Sudden increase in the number of COVID-19 patients causes a manpower shortage in medical institutions. Computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) system provides quick and quantitative diagnosis results. CAD system for COVID-19 enables efficient diagnosis workflow and contributes to reduce such manpower shortage. This paper proposes an automated classification method of chest CT volumes for COVID-19 diagnosis assistance. We propose a COVID-19 classification convolutional neural network (CNN) that has a 2D/3D hybrid feature extraction flows. The 2D/3D hybrid feature extraction flows are designed to effectively extract image features from anisotropic volumes such as chest CT volumes for diagnosis. The flows extract image features on three mutually perpendicular planes in CT volumes and then combine the features to perform classification. Classification accuracy of the proposed method was evaluated using a dataset that contains 1288 CT volumes. An averaged classification accuracy was 83.3%. The accuracy was higher than that of a classification CNN which does not have 2D and 3D hybrid feature extraction flows.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an automated CNN-based classification method for chest CT volumes to assist COVID-19 diagnosis. The method uses a 2D/3D hybrid feature extraction architecture that processes images on three mutually perpendicular planes and combines features for classification, achieving 83.3% average accuracy on 1,288 CT volumes, outperforming a CNN without the hybrid feature extraction flows.
AI.motivation: The rapid spread of COVID-19 has caused a surge in infected patients, leading to manpower shortages in medical institutions. A computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) system for COVID-19 can provide quick and quantitative diagnosis results, improving diagnostic workflow efficiency and alleviating the burden on medical staff.
AI.method: The paper proposes a COVID-19 classification convolutional neural network (CNN) with 2D/3D hybrid feature extraction flows. The flows are specifically designed to handle anisotropic volumes such as chest CT volumes by extracting image features from three mutually perpendicular planes within the CT volume and then combining these features to perform the final classification.
AI.result: The proposed method was evaluated on a dataset of 1,288 CT volumes and achieved an averaged classification accuracy of 83.3%, which was higher than that of a baseline classification CNN that does not include the 2D/3D hybrid feature extraction flows.
AI.conclusion: The 2D/3D hybrid feature extraction approach effectively improves COVID-19 classification accuracy on chest CT volumes, demonstrating its potential as a useful tool in computer-aided COVID-19 diagnosis systems.

title: Retrieval-Driven Training-Free AI-Generated Video Attribution
summary: AI-generated videos are becoming increasingly realistic and difficult to distinguish from authentic ones, which facilitates malicious misuse and poses growing threats to cybersecurity and social governance. Attributing AI-generated videos to their specific generative sources is therefore of critical importance for forensic investigation and legal regulation. However, most existing visual attribution methods focus on images and particularly rely on the image generation model, thereby lacking the ability to generalize to large-scale AI-generated video data. To address these limitations, we introduce an training-free AI-generated video attribution paradigm. Specifically, we formulates AI-generated video attribution as an instance retrieval task, and design a generative fingerprint-based pipeline. This pipeline consists of an adapted orthogonal color transformation, multi-scale quantized residual generation, and temporal-semantic aggregation, progressively capturing and integrating artifacts introduced by generative models across video frames. Extensive experiments on the GenVidBench benchmark demonstrate that our method achieves strong performance in both AI-generated video detection and attribution, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods with a Rank-1 accuracy of 20.5% and a mean Average Precision of 16.6%. The code is at https://github.com/renxi-seu/Video_Attribution.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a training-free paradigm for AI-generated video attribution, formulating it as an instance retrieval task with a generative fingerprint-based pipeline that captures artifacts across video frames, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the GenVidBench benchmark.
AI.motivation: AI-generated videos are becoming increasingly realistic, posing threats to cybersecurity and social governance. Existing visual attribution methods focus on images and lack generalization to large-scale AI-generated video data, creating a critical need for video-specific attribution approaches.
AI.method: The method formulates AI-generated video attribution as an instance retrieval task and designs a training-free generative fingerprint-based pipeline consisting of: (1) an adapted orthogonal color transformation, (2) multi-scale quantized residual generation, and (3) temporal-semantic aggregation, which progressively captures and integrates artifacts introduced by generative models across video frames.
AI.result: On the GenVidBench benchmark, the method achieves a Rank-1 accuracy of 20.5% and a mean Average Precision of 16.6%, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods in both AI-generated video detection and attribution.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training-free paradigm demonstrates that generative fingerprints can effectively attribute AI-generated videos to their specific sources, providing a scalable solution for forensic investigation and legal regulation without requiring additional model training.

title: Visual Distribution Anchoring for Efficient Prompt Tuning
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure
summary: Prompt tuning adapts vision--language models with few trainable parameters, but existing approaches trade off efficiency and adaptation: static textual prompts can overfit source classes, image-conditioned prompts add per-instance computation, and multimodal tuning modifies the visual branch. We propose VDA (Visual Distribution Anchoring), a training-free target adaptation framework that augments a frozen semantic classifier with class-level visual prototypes estimated offline from an unlabeled target pool. We first ask whether prototypes can be synthesized from class names. A text-to-centroid mapper reconstructs held-out source prototypes but fails under dataset shift because class names specify semantic identity, not target-domain appearance. An oracle analysis confirms that true target prototypes are highly discriminative. VDA therefore uses frozen semantic and domain-template classifiers to partition unlabeled target images into class-correlated groups. Confidence-ranked image features form normalized prototypes, fused with the semantic classifier using one global weight. Adaptation requires no target labels, target-side optimization, uniform class-prior assumption, iterative refinement, or test-query access, and yields a fixed, cacheable classifier. Controlled experiments show that class-specific partitioning drives gains and that visually local pseudo-label errors can remain useful despite being class-incorrect. Across ten ImageNet-to-target transfers, the same frozen design improves zero-shot CLIP, TCP, and MaPLe by 3.22, 3.39, and 3.35 points, respectively, improving nine of ten targets in every setting. Its visual correction further improves leakage-free PromptKD by 2.79 points, complementing zero-shot, source-prompted, multimodal-prompted, and target-distilled classifiers.

AI.tldr: VDA (Visual Distribution Anchoring) is a training-free target adaptation framework that augments a frozen semantic classifier with class-level visual prototypes estimated offline from an unlabeled target pool, improving zero-shot CLIP, TCP, and MaPLe across ten ImageNet-to-target transfers without any target-side optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt tuning approaches trade off efficiency and adaptation: static textual prompts overfit source classes, image-conditioned prompts add per-instance computation, and multimodal tuning modifies the visual branch, motivating a training-free adaptation approach that uses offline-partitioned target data.
AI.method: VDA uses frozen semantic and domain-template classifiers to partition unlabeled target images into class-correlated groups, then forms normalized prototypes from confidence-ranked image features, fused with the semantic classifier using one global weight. It requires no target labels, target-side optimization, uniform class-prior assumption, iterative refinement, or test-query access, yielding a fixed cacheable classifier.
AI.result: Across ten ImageNet-to-target transfers, the frozen design improves zero-shot CLIP, TCP, and MaPLe by 3.22, 3.39, and 3.35 points respectively, improving nine of ten targets in every setting. Visual correction further improves leakage-free PromptKD by 2.79 points.
AI.conclusion: Class-specific partitioning drives the gains, and even visually local pseudo-label errors can remain useful despite being class-incorrect, complementing zero-shot, source-prompted, multimodal-prompted, and target-distilled classifiers.

title: SafeNexus: Discovering and Steering Modality-Universal Safety Neurons in MLLMs
summary: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising safety performance, extending them to Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) exposes a significant gap between expanded multimodal capabilities and existing safety mechanisms. Current defenses remain predominantly confined to specific modal settings, thereby limiting their robustness against broader cross-modal threats. To bridge this gap, we introduce SafeNexus, a cross-modal safety alignment framework that adopts a dedicated neuron-level intervention strategy. First, we formulate a neuron localization paradigm that identifies functionally specialized neurons by characterizing intermediate-layer activation patterns and quantifying their functional salience through importance scoring. Building upon this paradigm, we exploit contrastive data to identify modality-bound safety neurons (BS-Neurons), and validate their role in regulating safety behavior within each modality via targeted suppression. Further cross-modal analysis defines modality-universal safety neurons (US-Neurons) as the shared subset of BS-Neurons identified across individual modalities, serving as the core for defending against harmful cross-modal attacks. We observe that suppressing these neurons substantially degrades safety performance across modalities, while leaving overall utility largely unaffected. Building on these insights, we propose two safety alignment strategies: activation-level safety amplifier and safety neuron calibrator. The proposed strategies enhance model safety through two distinct routes: the former amplifies the activation magnitudes of US-Neurons, while the latter selectively calibrates them via targeted fine-tuning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms prevailing state-of-the-art approaches on safety benchmarks spanning diverse modality combinations, while effectively preserving utility.

AI.tldr: SafeNexus proposes a cross-modal safety alignment framework for Multimodal LLMs using neuron-level intervention. It identifies modality-bound safety neurons (BS-Neurons) and modality-universal safety neurons (US-Neurons) through contrastive data, then applies two strategies—activation-level safety amplifier and safety neuron calibrator—to enhance safety across modalities while preserving utility.
AI.motivation: Extending LLMs to MLLMs reveals a significant gap between expanded multimodal capabilities and existing safety mechanisms. Current defenses are confined to specific modal settings, limiting robustness against cross-modal threats.
AI.method: (1) Neuron localization paradigm that identifies functionally specialized neurons via intermediate-layer activation patterns and importance scoring. (2) Contrastive data used to identify modality-bound safety neurons (BS-Neurons) and modality-universal safety neurons (US-Neurons). (3) Two safety alignment strategies: activation-level safety amplifier (amplifies US-Neuron activation magnitudes) and safety neuron calibrator (selective fine-tuning of US-Neurons).
AI.result: Suppressing US-Neurons degrades safety across modalities while leaving utility largely unaffected. The proposed strategies outperform state-of-the-art methods on safety benchmarks spanning diverse modality combinations while effectively preserving utility.
AI.conclusion: Neuron-level intervention on modality-universal safety neurons provides an effective route for robust cross-modal safety alignment in MLLMs, addressing the gap between expanded multimodal capabilities and existing safety mechanisms.

title: LegoQ: Density-Matrix Representation Learning with Spectral-Spatial State Transitions for Hyperspectral Classification
summary: Hyperspectral image classification is complicated by mixed pixels, spectral ambiguity, class imbalance, and limited annotations. Most current classifiers encode a pixel or patch as a deterministic vector and apply a linear or multilayer softmax head. Although effective for discrimination, this representation does not directly expose how mixed or uncertain a sample is. This paper presents \method, a classical density-matrix representation learning framework for hyperspectral images. The spectral bands are divided into groups and each group is mapped to a positive semi-definite, Hermitian, trace-normalized matrix state. A composable stack of spectral, spatial, and inter-group transitions then updates the states while repeatedly projecting them back to the valid state set. Instead of flattening the final features, \method\ aggregates the group states and compares them with learnable class-prototype density matrices through Uhlmann fidelity. The normalized eigenspectrum, von Neumann entropy, purity, and prototype fidelity provide sample-level diagnostics that are unavailable from a conventional vector head. On Indian Pines, ten runs yield an overall accuracy of $96.20\pm0.70\%$, an average accuracy of $95.57\pm1.29\%$, and a kappa coefficient of $95.66\pm0.80\%$. On WHU-Hi-LongKou, the best of ten runs reaches $97.52\%$ overall accuracy. Classification maps and feature projections show that the transition stack produces compact and better separated class structures. The results support constrained matrix-state learning as a practical alternative to vector-only hyperspectral classification without requiring quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a density-matrix representation learning framework for hyperspectral image classification. Spectral bands are grouped and mapped to Hermitian density matrices, which are updated through composable spectral, spatial, and inter-group transition layers while being projected back to valid state sets. Classification is done by comparing aggregated group states with learnable class prototype density matrices via Uhlmann fidelity. The method achieves strong results on Indian Pines (96.20% OA ± 0.70%) and WHU-Hi-LongKou (97.52% best OA), while providing sample-level uncertainty diagnostics (eigenspectrum, von Neumann entropy, purity, prototype fidelity) unavailable from conventional vector heads.
AI.motivation: Current hyperspectral classifiers encode samples as deterministic vectors with softmax heads, which fails to directly expose sample uncertainty, mixedness, or classification ambiguity—important given mixed pixels, spectral ambiguity, class imbalance, and limited annotations in hyperspectral imagery.
AI.method: The framework divides spectral bands into groups, maps each group to a positive semi-definite Hermitian trace-normalized density matrix, applies a composable stack of spectral, spatial, and inter-group transition layers with repeated projection back to the valid quantum-state set, then aggregates group states and compares them to learnable class-prototype density matrices using Uhlmann fidelity for classification.
AI.result: On Indian Pines across ten runs: 96.20±0.70% overall accuracy, 95.57±1.29% average accuracy, 95.66±0.80% kappa. On WHU-Hi-LongKou, the best of ten runs achieves 97.52% overall accuracy. Classification maps and feature projections demonstrate compact and better separated class structures.
AI.conclusion: Constrained matrix-state learning serves as a practical alternative to vector-only hyperspectral classification, requiring no quantum hardware while providing richer sample-level diagnostics and better class separation.

title: RAID: Towards Robust AI-Generated Image Detection with Bit-Reversed Images
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures
summary: The rapid advancement of image generation models has made it increasingly difficult for people to distinguish AI-generated images from real ones. To prevent the potential risks associated with the misuse of fake images, AI-generated image detection has gained significant attention. Existing methods neglect the inherent differences between real and fake images, thus lacking robustness and generalization ability. In this work, we innovatively investigate AI-generated image detection using bit-planes, and introduce the bit-reversed image. We propose a simple yet effective pipeline consisting of construction of bit-reversed images, gradient-based patch selection and a convolutional classifier. Besides, we provide a theoretical analysis from the mathematical perspective to demonstrate the validity of our approach. We also introduce two challenging datasets for AI-generated image detection. Extensive experiments verify the effectiveness of our approach across different settings, including cross-generator generalization, cross-dataset generalization and zero-shot performance. Without bells and whistles, our approach outperforms existing methods on over 40 benchmarks, and is nearly 100 times faster than counterparts. The code is at https://github.com/renxi-seu/RAID.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel AI-generated image detection method based on bit-planes, introducing bit-reversed images combined with gradient-based patch selection and a convolutional classifier. The approach demonstrates strong generalization, cross-generator robustness, and nearly 100x speed improvement over existing methods across 40+ benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-generated image detection methods neglect the inherent structural differences between real and fake images, leading to poor robustness and generalization. The authors aim to address this by leveraging bit-plane information that captures fundamental differences between real and synthetic images.
AI.method: The pipeline consists of three components: (1) construction of bit-reversed images from bit-planes, which reveal inherent differences between real and fake images, (2) gradient-based patch selection to focus on discriminative regions, and (3) a convolutional classifier for detection. The approach is supported by mathematical/theoretical analysis and validated on two newly introduced challenging datasets.
AI.result: The approach outperforms existing methods on over 40 benchmarks across cross-generator generalization, cross-dataset generalization, and zero-shot settings, while being nearly 100 times faster than competing methods.
AI.conclusion: Bit-plane based analysis provides a simple, theoretically grounded, and efficient solution to AI-generated image detection with superior generalization and speed compared to existing approaches.

title: Classification of COVID-19 cases from chest CT volumes using hybrid model of 3D CNN and 3D MLP-Mixer
comment: Accepted as a poster presentation in SPIE Medical Imaging 2023
summary: This paper proposes an automated classification method of COVID-19 chest CT volumes using improved 3D MLP-Mixer. Novel coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) spreads over the world, causing a large number of infected patients and deaths. Sudden increase in the number of COVID-19 patients causes a manpower shortage in medical institutions. Computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) system provides quick and quantitative diagnosis results. CAD system for COVID-19 enables efficient diagnosis workflow and contributes to reduce such manpower shortage. In image-based diagnosis of viral pneumonia cases including COVID-19, both local and global image features are important because viral pneumonia cause many ground glass opacities and consolidations in large areas in the lung. This paper proposes an automated classification method of chest CT volumes for COVID-19 diagnosis assistance. MLP-Mixer is a recent method of image classification using Vision Transformer-like architecture. It performs classification using both local and global image features. To classify 3D CT volumes, we developed a hybrid classification model that consists of both a 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) and a 3D version of the MLP-Mixer. Classification accuracy of the proposed method was evaluated using a dataset that contains 1205 CT volumes and obtained 79.5% of classification accuracy. The accuracy was higher than that of conventional 3D CNN models consists of 3D CNN layers and simple MLP layers.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an automated COVID-19 classification method for chest CT volumes using a hybrid model combining 3D CNN and an improved 3D MLP-Mixer, achieving 79.5% classification accuracy on a dataset of 1205 CT volumes.
AI.motivation: The rapid global spread of COVID-19 has caused a shortage of medical manpower. CAD systems can provide quick and quantitative diagnosis to improve workflow efficiency and alleviate this burden. Both local and global image features are important for diagnosing viral pneumonia including COVID-19, as ground glass opacities and consolidations appear in large areas of the lung.
AI.method: A hybrid classification model is developed that combines a 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) with a 3D version of the MLP-Mixer architecture. This leverages both local feature extraction (via CNN) and global feature modeling (via MLP-Mixer) for classifying 3D chest CT volumes.
AI.result: The proposed method achieved 79.5% classification accuracy on a dataset containing 1205 CT volumes, outperforming conventional 3D CNN models composed of 3D CNN layers and simple MLP layers.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid 3D CNN + improved 3D MLP-Mixer approach provides a viable CAD method for COVID-19 diagnosis assistance, demonstrating superior accuracy compared to conventional 3D CNN architectures with simple MLP classifiers.

title: Adjudicated Captioning: Multi-Agent Alignment Scoring and Consensus-Distilled Beam Arbitration for Strict Zero-Shot Image Captioning
summary:
Zero-shot image captioning (ZIC) describes images without paired image-caption supervision during captioner training, relying on text-only corpora and frozen pretrained image-text scorers. Existing retrieval-augmented methods score image-text alignment once, at retrieval, then commit the captioner's autoregressive beam under language-model probability alone, leaving the decoder without further visual grounding feedback. Progress has stalled, with no method improving on the strict-regime best since 2024.
  We propose Adjudicated Captioning, an inference-time multi-agent framework that restores grounding feedback at multiple checkpoints over an unchanged IFCap captioner. First, we install a stronger frozen Retrieval Encoder at the input. Second, between retrieval and decoding we insert a frozen Cross-Attention Verifier that re-ranks the top-9 retrievals to top-5. Third, at the output beam we attach a learned Reranker pairing TriFuse, a multilayer perceptron, with MemAttend, a memory-attended transformer, the pipeline's only learned components; both are trained self-supervised by Borda-consensus distillation across the three frozen scorers, using no paired image-caption labels and no reference captions.
  Under the inductive headline protocol, with rerankers fit on the disjoint COCO Karpathy validation beam and applied frozen to test, the framework reaches CIDEr 117.6 and SPICE 21.9 on COCO Karpathy, up from 108.0 and 20.3 for IFCap, a +9.6 CIDEr gain, and +7.7 above NES, the strongest synthetic-image-augmented method at 109.9, without retraining the captioner. A training-free fixed-fusion baseline reaches 115.8 CIDEr, so +7.8 of the +9.6 gain comes from the non-learned architectural intervention and the remaining +1.8 from the learned rerankers. The same recipe transfers off-COCO without captioner retraining: +8.1 CIDEr on Flickr30k Karpathy and +5.7 on NoCaps overall.

AI.tldr: Adjudicated Captioning is an inference-time multi-agent framework for zero-shot image captioning that restores visual grounding feedback at multiple checkpoints over an unchanged IFCap captioner, achieving +9.6 CIDEr on COCO Karpathy through a stronger retrieval encoder, a cross-attention verifier, and learned rerankers trained via Borda-consensus distillation without paired labels.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented zero-shot image captioning methods score image-text alignment only once at retrieval time, then commit the decoder's beam search under language-model probability alone without further visual grounding feedback. Progress has stalled since 2024, with no method improving on the strict-regime best.
AI.method: The framework inserts multiple grounding checkpoints over an unchanged IFCap captioner: (1) a stronger frozen Retrieval Encoder at the input, (2) a frozen Cross-Attention Verifier that re-ranks top-9 retrievals to top-5 between retrieval and decoding, and (3) a learned Reranker combining TriFuse (a multilayer perceptron) with MemAttend (a memory-attended transformer) at the output beam. The learned components are trained self-supervised via Borda-consensus distillation across three frozen scorers, with no paired image-caption labels or reference captions.
AI.result: Under the inductive headline protocol, the framework reaches CIDEr 117.6 and SPICE 21.9 on COCO Karpathy (up from 108.0 and 20.3 for IFCap), a +9.6 CIDEr gain and +7.7 above NES (the strongest synthetic-image-augmented method). A training-free fixed-fusion baseline achieves 115.8 CIDEr, showing +7.8 of the +9.6 gain comes from non-learned architectural intervention and +1.8 from learned rerankers. The recipe transfers off-COCO: +8.1 CIDEr on Flickr30k and +5.7 on NoCaps.
AI.conclusion: Adjudicated Captioning demonstrates that significant zero-shot image captioning gains can be achieved without retraining the captioner, by restoring visual grounding at multiple inference checkpoints. The approach is label-free, transfers across datasets, and shows the majority of gains come from architectural interventions rather than learned components.

title: CAER: Conflict-Aware Evidence Routing with Dual Prefix Experts for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in multimodal understanding and generation. However, when textual inputs conflict with visual evidence, they still suffer from hallucinations and produce responses inconsistent with visual content. Existing approaches mainly rely on decoding strategies, additional training, verification methods, or prompting techniques, but often lack fine-grained conflict localization and conflict-aware generation. In this work, we propose CAER, a backbone-agnostic framework for visual-language conflict detection and conflict-aware generation. CAER introduces a span-grounded evidence router that transforms claim representations into soft textual queries and retrieves corresponding evidence from frozen visual tokens, enabling fine-grained conflict estimation. Furthermore, we design a dual-prefix expert routing mechanism that learns separate experts for visually supported and contradicted inputs, enabling conflict-aware generation through explicit expert selection. Experiments on the public MMMC benchmark and our newly curated AgriConflict dataset demonstrate that CAER effectively detects visual-language conflicts and improves the reliability of open-source MLLMs without updating their backbone parameters.

AI.tldr: CAER is a backbone-agnostic framework for detecting visual-language conflicts in MLLMs and enabling conflict-aware generation through a span-grounded evidence router and dual-prefix expert routing, improving reliability without updating backbone parameters.
AI.motivation: MLLMs suffer from hallucinations when textual inputs conflict with visual evidence. Existing approaches (decoding strategies, fine-tuning, verification, prompting) lack fine-grained conflict localization and conflict-aware generation capabilities.
AI.method: CAER consists of two main components: (1) a span-grounded evidence router that converts claim representations into soft textual queries to retrieve evidence from frozen visual tokens for fine-grained conflict estimation, and (2) a dual-prefix expert routing mechanism that learns separate experts for visually supported and contradicted inputs, enabling explicit expert selection for conflict-aware generation.
AI.result: Experiments on the MMMC benchmark and the newly curated AgriConflict dataset show that CAER effectively detects visual-language conflicts and improves the reliability of open-source MLLMs without updating their backbone parameters.
AI.conclusion: CAER provides an effective, backbone-agnostic solution for detecting and handling visual-language conflicts in MLLMs, improving reliability through fine-grained conflict localization and conflict-aware generation without costly backbone fine-tuning.

title: SULAND v2: A Refined RGB Dataset and Deep Learning Object Detection Benchmark for UAV/UGV-Based SUrface LANDmine Detection Under Domain Shift
comment: The manuscript is currently under submission to a journal for peer review
summary: RGB imagery offers a practical, low-cost option for Unmanned Aerial/Ground Vehicle (UAV/UGV) survey support in surface-landmine detection, but object detectors remain underexplored in this safety-critical domain. Limited cross-architecture benchmarking and insufficient out-of-distribution (OOD) analysis obscure whether detectors generalize across deployment conditions. This challenge is amplified by the scarcity of public RGB landmine datasets, making SULAND a key benchmark for PFM-1 and PMA-2 detection. However, inspection reveals missing/false annotations, localization errors, inconsistent visibility criteria, visual artifacts, temporal labeling inconsistencies, and an inverted OOD class-ID convention in SULAND. We present SULAND_v2, a refined RGB surface-landmine dataset and benchmark. Preserving original images and splits, we manually revise annotations to ensure completeness, precise localization, label validity, and class consistency. SULAND_v2 contains 33,771 images and 12,433 bounding boxes. We benchmark 35 detector configurations across nine families. Annotation refinement improves YOLOv8 in-distribution (IID) test mAP@50 by 14.6-19.6 percentage points, while fixing the OOD class-ID convention increases mean YOLOv8 OOD mAP@50 by ~25 percentage points. On SULAND_v2, YOLOv12-Small achieves the highest IID mAP@50 (0.908), while RF-DETR-Large yields the strongest OOD performance (0.799 mAP@50, 0.675 recall). Our results demonstrate that high IID accuracy does not guarantee operational readiness. SULAND_v2 provides a reliable benchmark for evaluating domain-shift robustness in RGB-based mine-action survey support.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SULAND_v2, a refined RGB surface-landmine detection dataset and benchmark that fixes annotation errors, localization issues, labeling inconsistencies, and an inverted OOD class-ID convention in the original SULAND dataset. The authors benchmark 35 detector configurations across nine families, showing that annotation refinement improves YOLOv8 IID mAP@50 by 14.6-19.6 points and fixing the OOD convention increases OOD mAP@50 by ~25 points. YOLOv12-Small achieves the best IID performance (0.908 mAP@50), while RF-DETR-Large leads in OOD robustness (0.799 mAP@50), demonstrating that high in-distribution accuracy does not guarantee operational readiness.
AI.motivation: RGB imagery is a practical, low-cost option for UAV/UGV-based surface-landmine detection, but object detectors remain underexplored in this safety-critical domain. The scarcity of public RGB landmine datasets makes SULAND a key benchmark, yet it contains significant annotation errors, false/missing labels, localization inaccuracies, inconsistent visibility criteria, temporal labeling issues, and an inverted OOD class-ID convention—all of which undermine reliable evaluation of detector generalization across deployment conditions.
AI.method: The authors manually revise all annotations in SULAND while preserving original images and train/test splits, ensuring completeness, precise localization, label validity, and class consistency. They then conduct a comprehensive cross-architecture benchmark of 35 detector configurations across nine detector families, evaluating both in-distribution (IID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) performance on the refined dataset.
AI.result: SULAND_v2 contains 33,771 images and 12,433 bounding boxes. Annotation refinement improves YOLOv8 IID test mAP@50 by 14.6-19.6 percentage points, and fixing the OOD class-ID convention increases mean YOLOv8 OOD mAP@50 by ~25 percentage points. YOLOv12-Small achieves the highest IID mAP@50 (0.908), while RF-DETR-Large achieves the strongest OOD performance (0.799 mAP@50, 0.675 recall).
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that high IID accuracy does not guarantee operational readiness in safety-critical mine-action contexts. SULAND_v2 provides a reliable benchmark for evaluating domain-shift robustness in RGB-based mine-action survey support, filling a critical gap in this underexplored safety-critical detection domain.

title: Evaluation-Verification Reward for Consistent Multi-Reference Image Editing
summary: While recent image editing models have made rapid progress, multi-reference editing remains challenging, particularly in maintaining visual consistency across references and ensuring overall visual harmony. Reinforcement learning has proven highly effective for text-to-image generation and single-image editing, but its extension to multi-reference editing is hindered by the absence of suitable reward models that capture multi-image relational constraints. Moreover, naively using multimodal large language models(MLLMs) as zero-shot evaluators faces a key tension between hallucination-prone long-form reasoning and the limited deductive power of short-form judgments. We address these issues with a Multi-dimensional Evaluation-Verification Reward(EVR). EVR decomposes evaluation into distinct visual criteria; for each criterion, an MLLM Evaluator generates multiple candidate hypotheses, and a Verifier grounds each claim in concrete visual evidence to accept or reject it, producing reliable and fine-grained reward signals. Together with a scalable data pipeline, our method enables RL fine-tuning of off-the-shelf editors without architectural changes. Extensive experiments show substantial gains over the base Qwen-Image-Edit, improving consistency and harmony to match or surpass NanoBanana.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Multi-dimensional Evaluation-Verification Reward (EVR) for reinforcement learning fine-tuning of multi-reference image editing models, overcoming the lack of suitable reward models by decomposing evaluation into visual criteria with MLLM evaluators and verifiers that ground claims in concrete evidence.
AI.motivation: Multi-reference image editing faces challenges in maintaining visual consistency across references and overall visual harmony. Existing reinforcement learning approaches for text-to-image and single-image editing cannot be easily extended to multi-reference editing because there are no suitable reward models that capture multi-image relational constraints. Naive MLLM-based zero-shot evaluators suffer from a tension between hallucination-prone long-form reasoning and the limited deductive power of short-form judgments.
AI.method: The authors introduce EVR (Multi-dimensional Evaluation-Verification Reward), which decomposes evaluation into distinct visual criteria. For each criterion, an MLLM Evaluator generates multiple candidate hypotheses, and a Verifier grounds each claim in concrete visual evidence to accept or reject it, producing reliable fine-grained reward signals. This is combined with a scalable data pipeline to enable RL fine-tuning of off-the-shelf editors without architectural changes.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial gains over the base Qwen-Image-Edit model, with improvements in consistency and harmony that match or surpass the NanoBanana baseline.
AI.conclusion: The EVR framework provides a reliable reward signal for RL fine-tuning of multi-reference editors by mitigating MLLM hallucination through an evaluation-verification mechanism, enabling significant performance improvements without requiring architectural changes to existing editors.

title: SAM+D: Parameter-Efficient Dimensional Lifting of SAM-Family Models via Depth-Routed LoRA and Depth Shifting
comment: Accepted to ECCV2026
summary: Existing methods for adapting 2D foundation models such as SAM to 3D volumes either process slices independently---ignoring inter-slice context---or require substantial architectural changes and retraining. In this paper, we present \textbf{SAM+D}, a parameter-efficient framework that lifts SAM-family models by one spatial dimension---enabling 3D volumetric segmentation from 2D SAM and, for the first time via parameter-efficient fine-tuning, end-to-end 4D (3D+T) spatiotemporal segmentation from video-based SAM2---while keeping the vast majority of pre-trained parameters frozen. SAM+D introduces two lightweight, model-agnostic modules into frozen transformer blocks: (1)~\textbf{Depth-Routed LoRA (DRLoRA)} experts with learned routing for spatially adaptive low-rank updates, and (2)~\textbf{Depth Shift Modules (DSM)} for cross-slice feature exchange at zero additional parameter cost. Together, they provide volume-level context while tuning only ${\sim}$2.8\% of parameters for SAM and ${\sim}$3.7\% for SAM2. We evaluate SAM+D in two distinct settings, each lifting the base model by one spatial dimension: 3D segmentation, where SAM(2D$\,\to\,$3D) is evaluated on four CT benchmarks (KiTS, Pancreas, LiTS, Colon), and 4D segmentation, where SAM2 (2D+T$\,\to\,$3D+T) is evaluated on a cell tracking challenge (CTC) dataset (Fluo-N3DH-SIM+). In both settings SAM+D achieves competitive or superior results under the single-point prompt setting while using fewer trainable parameters than existing methods, demonstrating that SAM+D generalizes across SAM-family architectures, target dimensionalities (3D, 4D), and domains spanning medical imaging and bio-scene understanding. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/JerrySongCST/SAM-Plus-D.

AI.tldr: SAM+D is a parameter-efficient framework that lifts 2D SAM-family models to 3D and 4D segmentation by introducing Depth-Routed LoRA (DRLoRA) experts and Depth Shift Modules (DSM) into frozen transformer blocks, tuning only ~2.8-3.7% of parameters while achieving competitive results on CT and cell tracking benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for adapting 2D foundation models like SAM to 3D volumes either process slices independently (ignoring inter-slice context) or require substantial architectural changes and retraining. There is a need for a parameter-efficient approach that preserves pre-trained weights while enabling volumetric and spatiotemporal understanding.
AI.method: SAM+D introduces two lightweight, model-agnostic modules into frozen transformer blocks: (1) Depth-Routed LoRA (DRLoRA) experts with learned routing for spatially adaptive low-rank updates, and (2) Depth Shift Modules (DSM) for cross-slice feature exchange at zero additional parameter cost. This lifts SAM to 3D and SAM2 to 4D while keeping the vast majority of parameters frozen.
AI.result: SAM+D achieves competitive or superior results under single-point prompt settings across four CT benchmarks (KiTS, Pancreas, LiTS, Colon) for 3D segmentation and a cell tracking challenge (CTC) dataset (Fluo-N3DH-SIM+) for 4D segmentation, while using fewer trainable parameters than existing methods (tuning only ~2.8% for SAM and ~3.7% for SAM2).
AI.conclusion: SAM+D generalizes across SAM-family architectures, target dimensionalities (3D and 4D), and domains spanning medical imaging and bio-scene understanding, demonstrating a scalable parameter-efficient approach to extending 2D foundation models to higher-dimensional segmentation tasks.

title: GO-PRE: Goal-Oriented Next-Best-View Selection via Predictive Rendering Entropy for Active 3D Reconstruction
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Active 3D reconstruction relies on active view selection to maximize reconstruction fidelity under limited capture budgets. However, most existing methods rely on surrogate signals such as parameter uncertainty or geometric heuristics, but these signals are often misaligned with the ultimate goal: the fidelity of rendered predictions. We propose GO-PRE, a goal-oriented next-best-view selection framework that explicitly targets information gain in the prediction space. Specifically, we formulate the objective as maximizing the reduction of the average marginal predictive entropy over a user-specified target view manifold. GO-PRE supports interactive goal specification and yields an efficient acquisition rule that enables real-time computation of information gain. Extensive experiments across benchmarks demonstrate that GO-PRE consistently improves active reconstruction performance and provides more reliable uncertainty quantification compared to state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: GO-PRE is a goal-oriented next-best-view selection framework for active 3D reconstruction that directly maximizes information gain in the prediction space (reducing marginal predictive entropy over user-specified target views) rather than relying on surrogate signals like parameter uncertainty or geometric heuristics. It enables real-time acquisition and outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
